title: Attenuation and decibels
goals: Turn two echo heights into a difference in dB, and a dB change into a height ratio
Say what weakens ultrasound in a material: scattering, absorption and beam spread
Work out the loss from an attenuation coefficient and a path length, there and back
Estimate a material's attenuation from two back-wall echoes
Apply a transfer correction between a reference block and the part
summary:
Echo heights on a flaw detector are **amplitudes**, compared in **decibels**:

$dB = 20\log_{10}\frac{A_2}{A_1}$

- **+6 dB** doubles an echo; **−6 dB** halves it
- **+20 dB** is ten times; **+40 dB** a hundred times
- dB **add**: 6 dB then 6 dB is 12 dB, four times

Back from dB to a ratio: $\frac{A_2}{A_1} = 10^{dB/20}$. (For power and intensity it would be 10 log, not 20: echo heights are amplitudes.)

**What weakens the sound**:

- **beam spread**: in the far field the beam widens and its energy spreads over a bigger area
- **scattering**: grain boundaries and small inclusions send energy off in other directions; worse at **higher frequency** and with **coarse grain** (cast iron, austenitic stainless welds)
- **absorption**: energy turned into heat
- losses at the **couplant** and surfaces

Scattering plus absorption is **attenuation**, given as a coefficient $\alpha$ in dB per mm (or dB/m). Pulse-echo goes there **and back**, so the loss is $2\alpha d$.

**Measuring it**: the second back-wall echo has travelled one extra round trip ($2T$) compared with the first. The difference in dB, less a correction for beam spread, divided by $2T$, gives $\alpha$.

**Transfer correction**: a reference block and the real part couple and attenuate differently. Compare the same kind of echo on both; the dB difference is added to the gain so sizing is fair.

Higher frequency gives better resolution but more scattering: on grainy material, drop the frequency.

formulas.name: Decibels from two amplitudes
formulas.says: How many times bigger one echo is than another, on a log scale: 6 dB for each doubling.
symbols: the second echo's height (% screen height)

formulas.name: Ratio from decibels
formulas.says: Turn a dB change back into how many times taller or shorter the echo gets.
symbols: the change in decibels (negative for a drop)

formulas.name: Attenuation loss, pulse-echo
formulas.says: The loss is the material's dB per millimetre, times the distance there and back.
formulas.example: 0.02 dB/mm to a back wall 100 mm down: $2 \times 0.02 \times 100 = 4$ dB.

bench.task: On a flaw detector you are trained to use, measure back-wall echo heights on a calibration block and see dB at work.
check: Set the first back-wall echo to 80% screen height and note the gain
Note the heights of the second and third back-wall echoes
Work out the dB between the first and second: $20\log_{10}\frac{80}{h_2}$
Add 6 dB of gain: does each echo double (until it hits the top of the screen)?

cards.q: An echo sits at 80% screen height. You take 6 dB of gain off. Where does it end up?
cards.why: 6 dB is a factor of two in amplitude, so −6 dB halves the echo: 40%. Taking 6 off as if it were per cent (74%) is the usual slip.

cards.title: Decibels: comparing echo heights
cards.body:
Echo heights are **amplitudes**. To compare two, use **decibels**:

$$dB = 20\log_{10}\frac{A_2}{A_1}$$

$\log_{10}$ is the logarithm (the calculator's log key): it asks 'ten to what power gives this?'. Handy values:

- ×2 = **+6 dB**; ×½ = **−6 dB**
- ×10 = **+20 dB**; ×100 = **+40 dB**

The flaw detector's **gain** is in dB, and dB **add**: +6 then +6 is +12 dB, four times the height.
cards.more:
Why logs? Echoes range from huge (a back wall) to tiny (a small flaw deep down): a range of thousands. On a log scale that is a manageable 60 or 70 dB, and multiplying heights becomes adding dB.

Numbers: an echo at 20% next to one at 80%. The ratio is 4; $\log_{10} 4 = 0.602$; times 20 is 12 dB. Check: 6 dB doubles 20% to 40%, another 6 dB doubles it to 80%: 12 dB.

Why 20, not 10? Decibels were defined for power. Power goes with amplitude squared, and squaring inside a log is the same as doubling outside it: $10\log(A^2) = 20\log A$.

cards.q: One echo is at {a}% screen height, another at {b}%. How many dB higher is the first?
cards.why: Echo heights are amplitudes: 20 times the log of their ratio.

cards.title: From dB back to heights
cards.body:
To see what a dB change does to an echo, run the rule backwards:

$$\frac{A_2}{A_1} = 10^{dB/20}$$

- +12 dB: $10^{0.6} = 4$ times
- −20 dB: $10^{-1} = 0.1$, a tenth
- +3 dB: $10^{0.15} = 1.41$ times

To bring an echo at height $h$ up to a reference of 80%, add $20\log_{10}\frac{80}{h}$ dB.
cards.more:
The $10^{x}$ key on the calculator undoes log. Divide the dB by 20 first, then raise 10 to that power.

Numbers: a flaw echo at 25%, reference level 80%. $20\log_{10}\frac{80}{25} = 20\log_{10} 3.2 = 10.1$ dB. So the flaw is 10.1 dB below the reference; many procedures record exactly that number ('−10 dB to DAC').

The rules of thumb are enough for most work: every 6 dB is a doubling, every 20 dB a factor of ten.

cards.q: An echo falls by {db} dB. What fraction of its original height is left?
cards.why: For amplitudes, the ratio is $10^{dB/20}$; a fall is a negative dB.
cards.hint: Divide by 20, then 10 to that (negative) power.

cards.title: What weakens the sound
cards.body:
- **Beam spread**: beyond the near field the beam widens, so its energy is spread over a bigger area and each echo is weaker the further it travels. Not a property of the material.
- **Scattering**: grain boundaries and tiny inclusions send bits of the wave off in other directions. Grows quickly with **frequency** and **grain size**.
- **Absorption**: the material turns some of the vibration into heat.
- **Couplant and surfaces**: losses getting in and out.

Scattering and absorption together are the material's **attenuation**.
cards.more:
Shout across a field and your voice fades with distance even in still air: that is spreading. Shout across a field in thick fog and it fades faster, and in a forest the trees break it up: that is scattering. Soft furnishings soaking it up: absorption.

Fine-grained rolled steel attenuates very little at 2–5 MHz. Cast iron, and austenitic stainless welds with their big, columnar grains, scatter heavily: the back wall is weak and the screen fills with 'grass' (noise from grain reflections).

The cure there is a lower frequency (longer wavelength, less scattering), often 1 MHz, sometimes 0.5 MHz, at the cost of resolution.

cards.q: Which of these is a property of the material itself, rather than of the beam or the coupling?
options: Beam spread in the far field
cards.why: Scattering (with absorption) is the material's attenuation. Beam spread depends on the probe and the distance; couplant and crystal size are about the set-up.

cards.title: The attenuation coefficient
cards.body:
A material's attenuation is given as a coefficient $\alpha$ (alpha), in **dB per millimetre** (or dB/m). The loss grows in proportion to the distance travelled.

In pulse-echo the sound goes **there and back**, so to a reflector at depth $d$:

$$L = 2\alpha d$$

The value depends on the material, its grain, its temperature and the **frequency**: always quote $\alpha$ with the frequency.
cards.more:
Numbers: steel at 5 MHz, say 0.02 dB/mm. A back wall 100 mm down: $2 \times 0.02 \times 100 = 4$ dB of attenuation on the round trip, on top of beam spread.

The same steel at 10 MHz might be 0.08 dB/mm (scattering rises steeply with frequency): 16 dB to that back wall. And a coarse cast at 5 MHz could be 0.1 dB/mm: 20 dB: the back wall may vanish.

This is why a reference block of the same material and condition as the part matters: a block that attenuates less makes every flaw in the part look smaller than it is.

cards.q: A material attenuates ultrasound by {al} dB per mm. A reflector is {d} mm deep. How many dB are lost to attenuation, there and back?
cards.why: The sound travels {d} mm down and {d} mm back: 2 × {d} mm at {al} dB per mm.

cards.title: Measuring attenuation from back-wall echoes
cards.body:
On a plate of thickness $T$, the **second** back-wall echo has travelled one **extra round trip**, $2T$, compared with the first. So:

- measure the dB between the first and second back-wall echoes
- take off a correction for **beam spread** (from the probe's DGS diagram or a reference block of known low attenuation)
- divide what is left by $2T$: that is $\alpha$ in dB/mm

Ignoring beam spread over-estimates the attenuation, especially on thin plates and small probes.
cards.more:
Numbers: a 50 mm plate. First back-wall echo at 80%, second at 50%. $20\log_{10}\frac{80}{50} = 4.1$ dB over an extra 100 mm of path. If beam spread accounts for about 2 dB of that, attenuation is about 2.1 dB per 100 mm: 0.021 dB/mm.

Reflection losses at the back wall matter too: a clean, flat, parallel back wall reflects almost everything; a rough or corroded one loses some each bounce. That is why the measurement is made on good surfaces, and compared with a block of the same material.

cards.q: On a {t} mm plate, the second back-wall echo is {db} dB below the first. Beam spread accounts for {bs} dB of that. What is the attenuation coefficient, in dB/mm?
cards.why: The second echo has one extra round trip, 2T. Take off what spreading explains; the rest is attenuation over 2T.

cards.q: On the reference block, a reference echo reaches 80% screen height at 42 dB gain. The same kind of echo (a back wall at the same path) on the part needs 48 dB to reach 80%. A flaw in the part is then found at 40% with the scanning gain set from the block. How should the flaw be reported against the reference?

steps.show: $48 - 42 = 6$ dB: the part loses 6 dB more (coupling, surface, attenuation)
Scan at the block's gain plus 6 dB, so the part is assessed fairly

steps.ask: The flaw at 40% without the correction would have been…
steps.show: At the corrected gain it reads 80%: the same as the reference
At the reference level (0 dB to reference), not 6 dB below it

cards.why: Without the transfer correction the flaw looks half as big as it is. The correction is measured, not guessed, and recorded with the results.

cards.q: Why is the transfer correction needed at all, if the probe and flaw detector are the same?
cards.context: The block needed 42 dB, the part 48 dB, for the same echo.
cards.model: The reference level is set on a block, but the part is a different object: rougher surface, curved, painted, a different grain or temperature, a different couplant layer. Each loses some sound. If those losses are bigger on the part, every echo from it is weaker than the same reflector would give in the block, so flaws are under-sized. Measuring the difference on the same kind of echo and adding it to the gain puts the two on an equal footing.
points: Reference set on a block, not the part
More loss on the part makes flaws look smaller
Measure the difference and add it to the gain

cards.q: On a 40 mm plate the first back-wall echo is at 100% and the second at 50%. Beam spread accounts for about 3 dB. What is the attenuation?
cards.why: dB, correct for spreading, divide by the extra round trip.

cards.q: A flaw echo sits at {h}% screen height. How many dB of gain would bring it to the 80% reference level?
cards.why: The gain needed is the dB between where it is and where you want it.

cards.q: Comparing a 64% echo with a 16% one. One line is wrong. Which?
lines: So the first is 6 dB higher
cards.why: Echo heights are amplitudes, so use 20 log. 10 log is for power and intensity. Check: 6 dB would only double 16% to 32%, not to 64%.

cards.q: Testing a coarse-grained cast steel at 5 MHz, the back wall is weak and the screen is full of grass. What change usually helps most?
options: Drop to a lower frequency, such as 1–2 MHz
Turn the gain up by 20 dB
cards.why: Scattering rises steeply with frequency, and coarse grain scatters a lot. A lower frequency gets through with less loss and less grass. More gain amplifies the grass along with everything else.

cards.q: The gain is raised by {g1} dB, then by another {g2} dB. By how many times does an echo grow in height?
cards.why: dB add, so add first, then turn the total into a ratio. (Or multiply the two ratios: the same thing.)

cards.q: Why not always use the highest frequency probe available?
options: High frequencies cannot find flaws at all
The flaw detector's screen is too small for them
cards.why: High frequency gives short pulses and short wavelengths, so better resolution and smaller flaws found, but much more scattering, so less penetration. Choose the highest frequency the material lets through.

cards.q: An echo at {h}% screen height. You add {g} dB. Where does it end up, in %, if the screen did not limit it?
cards.why: Gain multiplies the height: turn dB into a ratio first. Adding dB to per cent directly is the slip.
cards.hint: Ratio from dB, then multiply the height.

cards.q: The second back-wall echo of a {t} mm steel plate (5920 m/s) appears how many µs after the first?
cards.why: One extra round trip, from the pulse-echo lesson. That same extra 2T is the path the attenuation is measured over.
cards.hint: One more round trip through the plate.

cards.q: Match each quantity with the right dB rule.
pairs: Two gain changes in a row
cards.why: Amplitudes: 20 log; powers: 10 log; and dB always add.

cards.q: An echo at 30% is raised by 6 dB. It is now at…
Echo A at {a}%, echo B at {b}%. dB difference?
α = {al} dB/mm, reflector {d} mm deep. Round-trip attenuation?
